group_hypergraph(): when membership is observed

honets

2026-08-26

The analytic question

A great deal of data is already group data. Authors on a paper. Students in a seminar. Codes applied in one session. Items in one basket. The group membership is recorded directly — nothing needs inferring.

The usual move is to project it to a pairwise network: everyone in a group gets connected to everyone else. That projection destroys information irreversibly. A five-author paper and ten separate two-author papers can produce exactly the same graph, and no analysis of the graph can tell them apart.

group_hypergraph() skips the projection. Each group becomes one hyperedge spanning all its members, and the group size survives into the analysis.

library(honets)
library(cograph)

Building one

Long-format data: one row per (member, group) observation.

hg <- group_hypergraph(human_long, member = "code", group = "session_id")
hg
Hypergraph: 9 nodes, 429 hyperedges
Size distribution:
  size_1   : 5
  size_2   : 3
  size_3   : 20
  size_4   : 32
  size_5   : 62
  size_6   : 77
  size_7   : 75
  size_8   : 75
  size_9   : 80
Source: group membership (member = code, group = session_id)

429 sessions become 429 hyperedges over the 9 action codes. The size distribution is the thing a pairwise projection would have thrown away: 80 sessions used all nine codes, while five used only one.

as.data.frame(hg, top = 4)
     hyperedge size
1 0086cabebd15    6
2 00bd84ef1666    3
3 00da7e5a052d    9
4 0162fe521f0c    9
                                                                             states
1                           Command, Frustrate, Inquire, Interrupt, Specify, Verify
2                                                       Command, Interrupt, Specify
3 Command, Correct, Frustrate, Inquire, Interrupt, Refine, Request, Specify, Verify
4 Command, Correct, Frustrate, Inquire, Interrupt, Refine, Request, Specify, Verify
  weight
1     NA
2     NA
3     NA
4     NA

A small worked example

df <- data.frame(
  person  = c("Alice", "Bob", "Carol", "Alice", "Bob", "Dave", "Carol",
              "Dave", "Eve"),
  session = c("S1", "S1", "S1", "S2", "S2", "S3", "S3", "S3", "S3"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
small <- group_hypergraph(df, member = "person", group = "session")
small
Hypergraph: 5 nodes, 3 hyperedges
Size distribution:
  size_2   : 1
  size_3   : 2
Source: group membership (member = person, group = session)
as.data.frame(small)
  hyperedge size            states weight
1        S1    3 Alice, Bob, Carol     NA
2        S2    2        Alice, Bob     NA
3        S3    3  Carol, Dave, Eve     NA

Three sessions, three hyperedges: a triple, a pair, and another triple. Note that S1 = {Alice, Bob, Carol} is one relation, not three.

Seeing it

splot(clique_expansion(hg), minimum = 0.05,
      title = "Group co-membership, projected")

Weighted membership

If the data record a quantity per (member, group) pair — hours contributed, messages sent, counts — pass the column as weight and the incidence matrix carries it.

dfw <- data.frame(
  person  = c("A", "B", "A", "A", "B"),
  grp     = c("g1", "g1", "g1", "g2", "g2"),
  n       = c(2, 5, 3, 1, 4),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
hw <- group_hypergraph(dfw, member = "person", group = "grp", weight = "n")
hw$incidence
  g1 g2
A  5  1
B  5  4

Repeated (member, group) pairs are summed: A appears twice in g1 with 2 and 3, giving 5. Without weight, the incidence is 0/1 and repeats simply collapse:

group_hypergraph(dfw, member = "person", group = "grp")$incidence
  g1 g2
A  1  1
B  1  1

Those edge-dependent vertex weights are exactly what hypergraph_centrality(type = "pagerank") and the Laplacian family consume — a weighted hypergraph carries information a binary one does not.

Missing values are dropped silently

dfn <- data.frame(
  person = c("A", "B", NA, "C", "D"),
  grp    = c("g1", "g1", "g1", NA, "g2"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
group_hypergraph(dfn, member = "person", group = "grp")
Hypergraph: 3 nodes, 2 hyperedges
Size distribution:
  size_1   : 1
  size_2   : 1
Source: group membership (member = person, group = grp)

Rows with NA in either column are removed before construction. Check your own missingness before calling — this verb will not warn you about it, and a silently shrunken hypergraph is easy to miss.

What the group structure buys you

m <- hypergraph_measures(hg)
as.data.frame(m, what = "global")
                 measure       value
1                n_nodes   9.0000000
2           n_hyperedges 429.0000000
3                density   0.7293447
4          avg_edge_size   6.5641026
5 pairwise_participation   1.0000000

Pairwise participation is 1.0: every pair of codes co-occurs in at least one session. A projected pairwise network would therefore be the complete graph on nine nodes — utterly uninformative, exactly as the first-order transition network is in the three-families comparison.

The hypergraph keeps its information because the hyperedges remain distinguishable by size and membership:

table(as.data.frame(m, what = "edges")$size)

 1  2  3  4  5  6  7  8  9 
 5  3 20 32 62 77 75 75 80

Naming

The argument is member, not player: the values become hypergraph nodes and need not be people — codes, items, genes and words are all common. The verb is named for what it returns (a hypergraph) rather than for its input format.

What to do next

  • hypergraph_measures() — hyperdegree, overlap structure and density.
  • hypergraph_centrality() — which members are central across the groups.
  • hypergraph_cluster() — group the members by the hypergraph’s own random walk.
  • clique_expansion() — the projection this verb avoids, when you deliberately want it.
  • window_hypergraph() — the sequence-based route to a hypergraph, when groups are local in time rather than given.

References

  • Perc, M., Gómez-Gardeñes, J., Szolnoki, A., Floría, L. M., & Moreno, Y. (2013). Evolutionary dynamics of group interactions on structured populations: a review. Journal of the Royal Society Interface, 10(80),
  • Battiston, F., et al. (2020). Networks beyond pairwise interactions. Physics Reports, 874, 1-92.
